utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the microphones, I must always remember microphones. I had a word with Mr. Margetts, who is dealing with this witness, and Mr. Tieger as well. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we not first have the case called?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't concentrating. I thought while we were dealing with things, that had been done. I'll sit down immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, these time constraints -- I like to get on with it, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. We had a brief word before the case was called to -- it would probably be helpful, it would save time if we were just to take a minute before the witness comes in to -- it's a sort of housekeeping matter in relation to this witness. Goodness, there's an echo this morning somewhere. About 25 in me in Court talking to myself. I'll manage, but I wonder if something could be done at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's simultaneous, it doesn't take extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour, but if it isn't, it tends to be repetitive. Your Honour, the position is that in the statements, as Your Honour will recall, and I'm thinking particularly of the long statement of this witness, the one that was signed in October 2002, he refers to a number of documents which he calls document 1, document 2, and so on. And in the interests of refining the matter, the position was taken by the Prosecution, I think in response to indications or requests from the Trial Chamber in relation to the 92 bis application and direction, those were whittled down to a smaller number and a list was given. But what we -- what we then have is a position where there are passages of the witness's statement which refer to documents which are now not being put in evidence. And in the discussion we had a few minutes ago, there are two directions one can go in relation to those passages, and I made it clear to the Prosecution, I'm not taking a particularly strong position about which direction one goes in. Either some of the passages linked to the, if you like, the missing documents have to be cut out of the statement or to make sense of some of those passages in the statement, some of those documents do in fact then have to be introduced. But what we can't have, we submit, is an intermediate situation where you've got bits of the statement referring to documents which are themselves not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in preparing the list of exhibits that we have now proposed to the Court, we were mindful to not include too many documents. We tried to limit it to the most important documents. Accordingly, in our review of the statement, we were mindful of that factor, and the other factor being that the statements had been admitted into evidence pursuant to the 92 bis ruling. So if we were to now proceed on the basis that if the attachments are not presented as exhibits, that the paragraph itself may be excised. We may need to review whether or not we should in fact introduce further attachments and maintain those paragraphs. So that would take us some time to conduct that review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, the witness will be here only for a short period of time. Of course, I think that the Defence might be interested to know which approach you choose, because that could influence their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you add exhibits, of course, they have to consider whether to put any additional questions on them, but of course, if you excise parts of the statement, then of course it would not. I think, as a matter of fact, since you've made your -- well, your preliminary choice as far as exhibits are concerned, that perhaps cutting those parts referring to exhibits not tendered at this moment would be the most appropriate way. But how much time would you need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a practical suggestion, which I hope wouldn't be inconvenient either to the Trial Chamber or to the Prosecution, which is that on our side, and we think subject to being able to find Mr. Gaynor in the building, it shouldn't be too difficult to proceed with the next witness, because I don't think Mr. Margetts is involved directly with the next witness. If that would give him the opportunity to do this exercise. Might I request, for example, Your Honour, that if we were, this would, I confess, be helpful to me, then if we were to designate, say, the beginning of one of the later sessions this morning. Because I would finish easily within a session with this witness. If, for example, we were able to bring him back at the beginning of one of the later sessions, it might be interrupting the next witness, but it would save time overall to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is that an acceptable suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it will take us that long to make the decisions on which attachments we'd like to introduce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to do it this morning? I take it that the witness doesn't -- that his flight will not depart before 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you later this morning what solution you've chosen. And the witness is still in The Hague. And presumably, no further questions might be needed, but if otherwise, then we always could recall the witness either later today or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, when Your Honour says no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean no further questions as a result of the choice made later this morning on what parts to take out of the statement or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is this: I don't think, and I say what I think at the moment is the right course because I'm trying to assess the way it's going. I don't think that the choice is made as to what should go in, what should stay out and so on. They're not likely to affect the overall length of the cross-examination. They might affect particularly which question I ask, as opposed to which question I don't ask. But Your Honour, the position is this: May I request this, that if I were able to start cross-examination at the latest at the very beginning of the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You delay at this moment this witness. And ask the next witness to be called --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, Your Honour, otherwise we should get in a bit of a tangle. It's just a question of clarity. The best course of all, Your Honour, because the last session is quite a short one, may I say the best course of all I suggest is, given what Mr. Margetts said about not needing much time, is if I could resume my cross-examination of this witness at the beginning of the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stewart has just raised this issue this morning and so I've had to think rather quickly as to how much time it will take us to make that review of the statement and determine whether we wish to introduce further exhibits. On reflection, I think if the Court adjourned for 10 minutes now, the Prosecution could respond to the Court and give an indication as to which paragraphs they wish to maintain and which paragraphs they're happy to excise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- Your Honour, I do suggest my suggestion is preferable because I'm bound to need at least a few minutes to consider the result of the ten minutes' work by the Prosecution. So it's going to save time if we do it the way I suggest and begin at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The beginning of the next session. That would be approximately 11.00. Would the Prosecution be in a position to call its next witness and that we start examining the next witness, then interrupt that for, well, say for approximately one hour, not more than one and a half hours, and then continue with the present witness? Who is going to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Gaynor will be taking the next witness and he is ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we expected to start perhaps in an hour and he could start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you please would be so kind to invite Mr. Gaynor to come to the courtroom and call your next witness. Which would be? First of all, no protective measures, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's Mr. Fejzija Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could then someone explain to Mr. Dzambasovic the reason why he is not called at this moment but that he'll appear at approximately 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask, just a very simple guideline. From what Mr. Margetts said about the time needed on a fairly informal understanding, if the Prosecution could please let me know, say, by 10.00 what their position is in relation to these matters and then I shall be ready by 11.00 then to proceed. There shouldn't be any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I hope Your Honours will forgive me if I do a little noisy tidying up of my stuff as I leave Court. It will only take me 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first thing we'll do is to check whether the next witness has already arrived. And make as much noise as you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But there's only one of me, I gather now the technical problem has been sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, you're on duty earlier than expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for this witness, I might give you a little bit of information as to how the examination will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This witness is a Rule 89(F) witness. We will be submitting three statements by him. One is an ICTY statement from 1991. Another is a Bosnian statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1991. ICTY. I have some difficulties in understanding that the ICTY was already --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In fact there's a typo in the first page which we will correct on the record. It's in 1999. And then there are two Bosnian statements which we'll submit as part of one package. The witness's evidence can really be divided into three parts in terms of time. The first part are events in late 1991 and early 1992, until the witness's arrest on the 25th of June. The second part of his testimony really relates to the period of his detention from the 25th of June until the 5th of August. And the third part of his testimony relates to the events of the 5th of August. Now, the Defence has informed us of objections in relation to four parts of the ICTY witness statement which I can identify now briefly for Your Honours. Paragraph 4 in its entirety. Paragraph 9, the sentence beginning with the words: "It is in my strong belief." Paragraph 25 in its entirely. Paragraph 26, the sentence beginning: "This was the start of the ethnic cleansing." We propose to examine the witness about those four parts of his statement in order to gather from him the facts which led him to form those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then in the statement that you'll tender, you take those parts out, so we have only the viva voce evidence on that, or -- because otherwise we get a bit confused, because then there is -- there are parts of the statement which are dealt with in the viva voce testimony. The objection is, as I understand, accepted by the Prosecution to the extent that it will cover those issues in the viva voce testimony rather than in the written statement. So therefore, we'd like to have it quite clear what parts of the statement, apart from having to look in the transcript what is admitted and what is not admitted as a statement. So we'd very much like to receive then a copy with those parts taken out to which the Defence objected and which objection has been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I might clarify the position. I informed the Defence that we did not consider that those paragraphs consisted of inadmissible evidence. We consider that those paragraphs are in fact admissible. Now, in respect of those paragraphs and indeed in respect of several other statements in the ICTY and Bosnian statements, there are expressions which require clarification and amplification by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's just get started. I take it that on the basis of the viva voce testimony, Ms. Loukas, you'll take a final position whether or not this could be kept in or whether it has to be taken out. Of course, if it's fully supported by viva voce testimony, one could wonder whether it's worth the exercise to take it out. Perhaps we just wait and see what happens in the examination and then give a final decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm happy to adopt that approach. At this stage I still maintain my objection to the matters that I've outlined to the Prosecution. And also I have one further objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will indicate, Your Honour. I've received a supplemental information sheet yesterday from the Prosecution with additional material from the witness, and which of course includes that from a particular meeting that this Grujo Lalovic person indicated that he had received orders from above, and referred to orders received from Trebinje. Now, and in addition to that, it's indicated that the additional supplemental information sheet indicates that the witness has suffered from PTSD, post-traumatic stress disorder. Now, Your Honour, of course, in the circumstances, and this is happening rather often, that when the witnesses come, there's this little addition, 12 years after the event, of orders from above. When one looks, Your Honour, at section 89 of the Rules, in terms of a Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, that's 89(D), Your Honour, how probative a piece of evidence would be emerging 12 years after the event is, Your Honour, a matter of great conjecture, firstly. And secondly, when one also takes into account the fact that the Statute includes ensuring protection of witnesses under Article 22, this is a witness for whom, Your Honour, there wouldn't be a great deal of cross-examination on what I've seen thus far. But when we have the additional - 12 years after the event - orders from above, I, as the Defence, Your Honour, am placed in the situation of cross-examining a witness with post-traumatic stress disorder about something that 12 years after the event has emerged. So, Your Honour, in those circumstances, I would be submitting that Your Honours would exercise your discretion to not allow this additional bit of evidence that's contained in the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also exclude, in the opinion of the Defence, any viva voce examination of -- on that subject or just --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: On this particular subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not only the statement but also to put questions to the witness in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. When one considers the balancing exercise that has to be performed by Your Honours in terms of Rule 89(D), I would submit that it's not automatic that evidence of this sort should go in, particularly 12 years after the event and particularly considering a witness who has, it appears, suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have considered your objection. Mr. Margetts -- Mr. Gaynor, I'm still in a situation five minutes ago. Mr. Gaynor, the Chamber will allow you to examine the witness on that subject, but will not accept the specific part mentioned by Ms. Loukas as a written statement, not as written statement evidence. Ms. Loukas, one of the reasons is that even if it emerges 12 years later, then that also could be because certain aspects that had less relevance, perhaps, in the eyes of who interviewed the witness at that time might be that they had no specific idea on to use that evidence, in what case. So therefore, it could well be a matter of relevance. And of course, the Chamber will pay specific attention to what you told us about the post-traumatic stress disorder in order to assess as good as we can whether the evidence is influenced by any such stress disorder. Of course, the Chamber is also aware that if a post-traumatic stress disorder would make a witness unfit to testify, then we might lose a lot of witnesses in this Court. And this is not to say that we ignore it, but the Chamber does not take the view that a PTSD in itself would disqualify a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor are you then ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I am indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Hadzic. I have to inform you, first of all, that the counsel for the Prosecution will start your examination this morning, but we'll then have an interruption for approximately one hour, one hour and a half, where we have to finish the testimony of another witness who had started already. So it will not be uninterrupted, your testimony. It will be interrupted later this morning. So you're prepared for that. You'll first be examined by Mr. Gaynor, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to ask you a few questions about your background. I'll just read a few sentences and I'd just like you to confirm that that information is correct with a yes or a no. You are from the village of Mjehovina near Kalinovik town in Kalinovik municipality. You served in the JNA in 1966 and 1967. In the spring of 1992 you were the director of the public utilities commission in Kalinovik. You're now retired and you have a wife and three adult children. Is that correct? Sir, can you hear what I said to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, Madam Usher, could you perhaps please check whether the witness receives -- whether he is on the right channel. Is the witness on the right channel? MR. GAYNOR:

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you some information about yourself and if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you now hear what Mr. Gaynor says in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. I understand everything. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, perhaps, since you might have read quite quickly, that the translation took quite some extra time before it was finished. So perhaps we should have some patience. Did you follow what Mr. Gaynor told you, the information he presented to you, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard everything. I'd just like to correct something. I was director of the public utilities company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where it says public utilities commission you say it was the public utilities company in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, everything was correct, what Mr. Gaynor said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender now the 89(F) package, consisting of three statements by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I'd like that package to be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P285.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose to read out now a summary of the evidence of the witness. This witness is from the municipality of Kalinovik. The harmonious multi-ethnic way of life in the municipality began to change in 1990 and 1991, with the arrival of a large number of JNA soldiers to the local artillery camp to prepare for deployment to Slovenia and Croatia. At the same time, there was a gradual increase in Serb nationalism and this began to filter into daily life. Later, the witness noticed that the JNA soldiers began wearing new uniforms bearing Serb insignia. At the municipality building, Serb flags were flown. When drunk, JNA soldiers began to fire their weapons into the sky and to take random potshots at the mosques. The witness considered that this behaviour was intended to intimidate the Muslims. The Muslims were unarmed and were not in a position to challenge the behaviour of the JNA soldiers. The SDS began to dominate local politics, and the witness was aware of several visits by Radovan Karadzic to the area. Relations between the SDS and the SDA deteriorated. It became apparent to the witness that the JNA had begun to arm local Serbs. The arming began as a covert operation, but later JNA trucks would drive around Serb villages, dropping off weapons at homes. Units of volunteers made up of local Serbs were formed. In April or May of 1992, the witness became aware that Serb artillery guns had been positioned with the barrels directed at the Muslim village of Golubici. A complaint was made to General Ratko Mladic, who was from the village of Bozanovici, clear Kalinovik town. The witness heard that General Mladic promised that the Muslim villagers would be safe. The guns were moved away, but in August 1992, the same guns were put back into the same positions and were used to bombard the village. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond A Muslim police commander and his Muslim colleagues were instructed to sign a declaration of loyalty to the Serbs. The Muslim police officers refused to do so and were told to hand in their weapons, which they did. Subsequently, the Serb police began to make arrests for no reason. The witness felt that life had become totally intolerable in Kalinovik as a result of the campaign of Serb intimidation. Serb SDS representatives would assure the non-Serbs that everything would be all right; on the other hand, Serb authorities would continue arrests and harassment. On 25th of June, 1992, a large number of Muslims received written notice to report for work duties. The witness and many other Muslims responded to this summons and appeared before the Kalinovik Municipal Assembly, where they were told to await the arrival of Grujo Lalovic, president of the SDS in Kalinovik and president of the executive committee. There was a strong police presence around the Municipal Assembly building and police had blocked all surrounding roads. Those Muslims who had responded to the summons, as well as some who had failed to respond, were rounded up and taken by police to the Kalinovik elementary school, where they were detained until the 6th of July, 1992. Gojko Lalovic, chief of civilian defence for Kalinovik, came to the school and told the Muslim detainees that they were being detained for their own safety and would soon be released. On the 6th of July, 1992, the detainees were moved under heavy security to an empty gunpowder magazine at Jelasacko Polje where they were detained under heavy guard. The witness was detained there for almost a month. On the 1st of August, 1992, detainees at the gunpowder magazine heard automatic gunfire and saw through the doors of the gunpowder magazine that Muslim houses were on fire in the hamlet of Karaula, in the village of Jelasca [phoen]. The witness saw women, children, and the elderly from the village being marched across Jelasacko Polje towards Kalinovik. On the following day, the detainees saw that Muslim houses in the village were continuing to be set afire. A man delivering water to the detainees told them that all the Muslims from neighbouring villages had been detained at Kalinovik elementary school. On the 5th of August, 1992, a group of around 15 detainees were called out from the gunpowder magazine and taken away. Later on the same day, the witness and other detainees were told that they were going to be exchanged. The guards took all valuables from the detainees, tied the hands of the detainees behind their backs with wire, and severely beat many of them. The detainees were loaded onto a vehicle, then unloaded, beaten, and then reloaded onto the trucks. A convoy of three trucks containing detainees, escorted by a police car, set off on a road towards Foca. The first truck in the convoy was being driven by a Muslim and contained no Serb guards, lest there be any land-mines on the road. During the trip, detainees on the witness's truck were forced by Serb guards to sing Serb nationalist songs. The convoy stopped at Ratine in Foca municipality, where all the detainees except the witness were executed. The witness will testify about that killing incident. The witness's testimony is relevant to killing 9.1 of schedule B to the indictment, to detention facilities 18.2, 18.3, and 18.4, mentioned in schedule C to the indictment, and to the mosques 14.1.and 14.2 in schedule D to the indictment. Could the witness be shown the first exhibit, please. And I would ask for an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P286.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, on your left, or on the screen in front of you, you have a map, and on that map are marked two locations, A and B, as well as your signature. Could you tell the Court what A is and what B is.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: The A is where the gunpowder depot magazine was, and point B is Ratine where they killed the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about a statement you made in your statement. There's no need to consult your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is paragraph 4 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said, and I quote: "It is my belief that all of the actions carried out to the people of Kalinovik by the Serbs were part of a greater plan controlled at a very high level --"

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just at this point, I might object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd rather have this to be put to the witness without reading his statement first, is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. If what the Prosecution seeks to do is establish the basis for that particular paragraph, then it's for the Prosecution to establish the basis rather than to read out the impugned paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I said that I expected the Prosecution to deal with these elements in viva voce testimony, then of course first reading that part of his statement might not be the appropriate way of approaching the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In that case, I'll clarify the objections by the Defence at the end of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to refer Your Honours to paragraph 23 of the ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your ICTY -- in your statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, you referred to a visit by a Chetnik group, and you said that when that Chetnik group arrived in Kalinovik, you became so frightened that you got ready to leave. But you were then reassured by SDS representatives that the Chetniks were under SDS control --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to get to the point where the Prosecutor wants to refer the witness to a particular aspect of his statement does not require reading out the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a matter of efficiency rather than, I take it -- let me just see. Yes, Mr. Gaynor. If you would -- if it is a subject that needs further elaboration in viva voce testimony, of course it depends a bit on what it is, whether it's a starting point where further details will be asked, then it might be a correct way of repeating the statement of the witness, because that's the starting point for the real questions. But, of course, if it is -- if you want to deal with the statement itself, so not seeking further details, but either seek a variation or -- then could you please, very cautious. So I'm not instructing you not to read, but it very much depends on -- if reading would provide the answer to the next questions, then it might be inappropriate to read. If, however, reading out part of his statement would be the introduction to what then follows, you may read as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In this case, there are certain elements which are unclear from the statement, and so I'm trying to draw very relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's appropriate to read first and to ask of certain parts of that statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So, Witness, as I was saying, there was a visit by what you describe as a Chetnik group, and you were reassured by SDS representatives that the Chetniks were under SDS control. My first question is: When was this?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: That occurred sometime around the 5th and 6th of May, 1992, when, in Kalinovik, a group arrived. They were armed. Chetniks from Miljevina, with Pero Elez. At the time we were in a panic and we tried to leave and escape from the village. At that point in time Grujo Lalovic arrived, who was president of the municipal SDS and president of the municipal board of the local assembly and president of the Crisis Staff. Yes, I'll slow down. And he told us that we would be safe. He guaranteed our safety and security if we stayed. He said nothing would happen to us. And at that meeting he drew our attention to the fact that we would have to give over -- hand over all our weapons and that we will be even safer then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you referred there to a meeting with Mr. Lalovic. On what date was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I think that was the 5th of May, 1992, towards evening. Otherwise, I had business relations with Lalovic, because he was in the Executive Board and I was in the utilities company which came under the municipality as a public company.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you personally attend the meeting of the 5th of May, 1992, with Mr. Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And all the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you -- when he -- in your statement you said that you were reassured that the Chetniks were under SDS control. Who made that assurance to you?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Grujo Lalovic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did the Chetniks remain in Kalinovik after that date?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. They went to Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you form the impression that Mr. Lalovic and the SDS did or did not have control over that Chetnik group?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the formulation of the question. The basic evidence that the Prosecution would seek to obtain from the witness, of course, is based on what he saw, heard, and what he witnessed. To ask a witness about his impressions is really not particularly probative. It's best to have the evidence that he relies on for his impressions and then the Trial Chamber can determine whether or not there is a basis for the impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, it's of no use to ask on the basis for an impression if there's no impression at all. So I don't think it's an inappropriate question. But it's certainly true that if the witness would say yes or no, especially if he says yes, that it would need further exploration to find out what the factual basis for that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But even in that format, Your Honour, I would argue that it's leading. Even though it says tell me whether you got that impression or not, Your Honour, it conveys the answer that the Prosecution wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's inadmissable leading, but Mr. Gaynor, you could have sought the approach to go first to the facts and then some build-up so we would then understand whether the witness had formed such an impression, yes or no. But I'm not disallowing you to put the question in this way. So the question is whether, apart from being told that the Chetniks were under SDS control, whether you have observed any facts which would support what was told to you in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it did go towards that assertion, bearing it out, because that same day, the people left Kalinovik and the next day there was nobody there. There were just the uniformed people that we know from Kalinovik, but nobody from outside, from other parts. So probably that was why I gained the impression that they were under the control of the SDS and the Crisis Staff of the Kalinovik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell the Court what precisely Mr. Lalovic said at the meeting of 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: He said precisely that he guaranteed our personal safety and security, that our lives would not come under threat or the lives of our families or our property, that we could go to work quite normally, work normally, and go about our business and implement the legal provisions enacted by the Municipal Assembly. So I continued to do my job normally. I continued to cooperate with people from the municipality and leadership. And I gained the impression that the situation would be all right and that nothing would happen to us. Because we had been given guarantees of that kind for our safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he say that he was speaking on behalf of himself, on behalf of the SDS, or on whose behalf was he speaking?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: He said that he was speaking on behalf of the body he represented, the municipal board of the SDS and the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Kalinovik and all the institutions that come under the Executive Board itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he say whether, yes or no, those bodies were receiving guidance from anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I would object on the basis that this is being proposed in a leading format. Just to add yes or no does not detract from leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not inadmissible leading. The objection is rejected. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my question to you. Did Mr. Grujo Lalovic say whether, yes or no, those bodies were receiving guidance from anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: From where did he say?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that he was receiving guidance and instructions as Kalinovik belonged to the SAO of Trebinje at that time. That means from that level of the autonomous region, from Trebinje, Mr. Vucurevic, they were receiving all the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown the next exhibit, please, and I'd like that exhibit to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P287.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate dated the 8th of September, 1992, when I handed over my personal weapons to the police of Kalinovik and everybody received confirmation and a certificate of this kind once they had handed in their weapons, their personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any mistake --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps the witness said the 8th of September, which causes me some problems to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you inspect the date of that receipt once again and confirm the date on it.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I misspoke. A slip of the tongue. It was the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That solves the month, but not the day. Could you -- perhaps I have to look at the original in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you once again inspect the date and clarify.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say it was a 9 and not an 8. I have the original. It's a poorer copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That will do. It's not a major issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, from this receipt, it appears that you surrendered a pistol. Did you keep any weapons that you did not surrender?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Among the Muslims in your village, did they give up their weapons also?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know of any Serbs who gave up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During what period, approximately, did the Muslims give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: That was in the beginning of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why did you all agree to give in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we agreed because it was said that they would search us, look for weapons, and that would be safer for us if we surrendered our weapons. Because it was obvious that with one pistol or one rifle, we couldn't hurt anyone but could only deteriorate the situation that was already tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement - I'd like to refer Your Honours to paragraph 16 of the ICTY statement - in your statement, sir, you refer to the arming of the Serb population, and you say that JNA trucks would drive around Serb villages, dropping off weapons at people's homes. My first question is: Did you personally see JNA trucks driving around Serb villages, dropping off weapons?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: There was one occasion when I was going on tour to see the local waterworks. In front of a house in a village, I saw a military vehicle and I saw crates with ammunition and with weapons being unloaded in front of that house. That house was about a hundred metres from where the water pipes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the person living in that house?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I know because Kalinovik is a small town. I knew every house, every owner of the house, and even every child living in each house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents which caused you to believe that the JNA was arming the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, there were. But let me go back to the Serbian Christmas and new year, when in the villages around Kalinovik, there were more rounds shot than during some combat. They had so many weapons, and everybody was using them in this celebratory shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that the Serbian Christmas and new year in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to refer you to paragraph 17 of the ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you said that you saw artillery directed at the village of Golubici and that a complaint was made to General Ratko Mladic. Who made that complaint to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: We complained to him when he came to his birthplace. He arrived in a helicopter and we learned that Velibor Ostojic was with him. He invited the Muslim residents of the Golubici village, who were right next to Bozanovici village and he talked to them and they complained directly to him. On that same day, he ordered that the artillery weapons be removed. However, the weapons, the anti-aircraft gun above my village remained there. I did not attend that meeting, but I heard about it from a lot of people, including my neighbours and the Orthodox Serbs who told me that they had been at that meeting and that Mladic said that to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery trained on Serb villages or Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to direct you to paragraph 13 of the ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you were aware of visits to Kalinovik by Radovan Karadzic. How were you made aware of these visits?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I heard about it from a member of the municipal council of the SDS who had business contacts with me. He told me that he came during the founding stage. And since I was in the utility company, I was involved in all these preparations that needed to be carried out. I was involved in all of that. And this man told me that on a few occasions Mr. Karadzic came to Kalinovik to establish the municipal council -- the municipal board of the SDS. However, I personally did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown the next exhibit, please, and I'd request an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P288.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see from this exhibit, this is a record of a conclusion made by the war staff of the Kalinovik Municipal Assembly at a session held on the 17th of May, 1992, to check up on military-aged men of Muslim nationality resident in Kalinovik municipality. This document states that they are to report to the secretariat for national defence between the 20th of May, the 25th of May, 1992. Did you personally report to the secretariat for national defence between the 20th and the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: As I did have my wartime assignment, I had a wartime obligation which was to continue working at the utility company throughout the war, did not report, because there was no need for me to report. But all other Muslims who were there and who had different wartime assignments did report to the municipal office of the secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you see in the last paragraph of that document it says: "After they have reported to the secretariat for national defence, they shall be prohibited from leaving the municipality without permission and they shall be obliged to report to the public security stations at Kalinovik, Ulog and Dobro Polje twice a week." Did you personally report to any public security stations?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I reported to the public security station in Kalinovik twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, please, and I'd request a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would that be 289, I take it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in this document dated the 11th of June, 1992, you see that Commander Colonel Ratko Bundalo states: "On the basis of the decision of the staff of the command of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and he goes on to order, in paragraph 1: "The territory of the municipalities of Kalinovik and Trnovo is declared a war zone." In paragraph 3, he forbids the entry of civilians into the region where combat activities are under way. My question is this, sir: On or around the 11th of June, 1992, which parts of Kalinovik, in your experience, were the locations of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, in Kalinovik municipality, there were no combat operations. There were such operations in Trnovo municipality and Nevesinje municipality, because this is where volunteers from Kalinovik went. In the territory of Kalinovik, there were no combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of that document, it states: "Movement of the population on the territory in the zone of combat activities, without the prior approval of the TG command, is restricted." My question is: Were you personally free to move around Kalinovik at this time, around the municipality?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: As for the movement around Kalinovik, it was quite safe, and I went around doing my work. However, it was not possible to go towards Ljut, Konjic, and some others, because there were artillery positions and defence positions along those roads. So these were the areas where movement was barred. The Muslim population who wished to leave Kalinovik could not receive a permit to leave it, and some people tried to go through the forest and leave the place, whereas those that remained had a different fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said there that the Muslim population who wished to leave could not receive a permit to leave the municipality. What about the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they lived there. There was no need for them to leave Kalinovik and go in the directions in which the Muslims went. Normally they went to Foca, Nevesinje, Gacko. Those were the directions that they travelled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that the Muslim population wished to leave Kalinovik. Why did the Muslim population wish to leave Kalinovik? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, the situation had changed. There were a lot of troops arriving into Kalinovik, and us Muslims, we could not receive humanitarian aid. So we could feel that there was no life for us there any more. Those who were afraid, they left the area, and those who were less afraid remained there and met their death there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that Muslims were afraid. Why exactly were they afraid? Was it merely the absence of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. But there were no Muslim representatives in the authorities who could ensure our protection. The public security station was mono-ethnic. All other bodies within the municipality as well. All Muslims who were employed in those organs and who had information from above available to them were not allowed to continue working there any more, not in the public accounting office, not in the secretariat for national defence. All people who had weapons and who were employed as security guards were informed that they should not report to work any more, that they should be on stand-by. Therefore, people were losing their jobs and it was everywhere. We could see it and we realised that our life there was not safe any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is headed: "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kalinovik municipality, municipal secretariat for national defence," and it's dated the 25th of June, 1992. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received such a document myself, but I lost it during the war. However, I did receive it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was the document you received the same as this document, apart from the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Same documents were sent, and they were the same documents and only names were entered manually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When did you receive the notification?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I received this notification on the 25th of June, 1992, at around 1.00 p.m., when I returned on that day home a bit earlier, I found this notification waiting for me there to report to the secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know who delivered it to your house?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I saw Gojko Lalovic taking this notification to other people. He had a driver with him, Badnjar Mihajlo, called Miha.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said in your Bosnian statement of 1993, paragraph 1, that after you received a summons bearing the signature of Nedzo Banjanin, you reported to the municipal assembly building and that there was a strong police presence around the Kalinovik Municipal Assembly building. Do you remember what kind of insignia the police were wearing, if any?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, active policemen had the regular uniform that they all had before the war, whereas reserve policemen had a winter blue uniform. They had blue berets with a tricolour flag on it. I knew all those people, because we used to work together, we grew up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What ethnicity were those policemen?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that while you were detained at the Kalinovik elementary school there were a number of police and other guards there. What ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph -- I'd like to direct Your Honours to paragraph 3 of the Bosnian statement of the 19th of February, 1993. Sir, you said that on the 1st of August, 1992, while you were being detained at the gunpowder magazine, you could see women, children, and the elderly being marched from the village of Jelasca [phoen], across Jelasacko Polje. How far away from those women, children, and the elderly from you?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: They were about 500 metres away from us. And when they approached the depot itself, we didn't see them because they were on the other side. But this is where they boarded the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the women, children, and the elderly?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I know because my wife is from that village, and those people were all my wife's relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just say very briefly which relatives of your wife were among those people.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: There was my wife's mother, her two sisters, her aunt and their families, aunts, uncles, their children, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that on the 2nd of August, 1992, they continued setting fire to Muslim houses in Jelasca [phoen]. Now, how did you know that those were Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that village. In addition to that, most of the people imprisoned were from that village, so they would say, you know, that house belongs to that person and that house belongs to that person. I myself knew all of those houses. We could see that through the openings in the steel door, through the bars, and also through the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take you to the 5th of August of 1992. You've described in some detail in your statements that you left in a convoy with an escort of a police car, the ammunition magazine at Jelasacko Polje, until you arrived at Ratine in Foca. Now, taking it up from the moment that you arrived that the convoy stopped at Ratine what happened when that convoy stopped?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: When the convoy stopped, uniformed men who were in the convoy escorting us got out and ordered us to descend the vehicles and not even try to escape, otherwise they would shoot us. We were extremely exhausted because we were not allowed to sit in the vehicle. We were just thrown in. So we got off, and at that moment a soldier in a uniform came and said that everything was ready. He had just gotten out of the stable. And in front of that vehicle, I saw a relative of mine who was completely bloody. He was not with us in a vehicle. He was in another vehicle. I saw some prisoners there. I recognised some of them, and we headed towards the stable in a column, one by one. When we got there, they selected four young men and they told them to turn their backs to us, and when they did that, they started shooting bursts of fire at us. I was hit by a bullet below my knee and I fell down and pretended to be dead. When they finished shooting, figuring that all of us were dead, they untied the hands of those four young men and ordered them to throw us into the stable and after that they would free them. The young men started doing their job. They threw me into the stable. And since there was some soil there on the ground, I was able to move as they were throwing more people in, I was moving to the side so that these corpses would not come on top of me. When they finished throwing us dead people in there, they again brought a man whom I believe to be that relative of mine whom I had seen all bloody. They shot him, and then they killed three of the young men who threw our bodies into the stable. And they left the fourth one alive. They ordered him to pour petrol over our bodies. He refused to do that. Then they shot him. And then they threw a rubber, burning rubber, into the stable. And when they saw that the fire started, they left. They got into their vehicles and left. When I heard that they had left, I managed to get up, and I stayed in the bottom of this stable, where there was an opening. And when I figured out that I was safe, I escaped from the stable. I got to the brook and I tried to untie my hands. I was unable to do that. But then I found a branch, and with the help of that branch, I untied my hands. You can still see the traces of wires around my wrists. I also had a wound on my head, near my eyebrow. I managed to dress my wounds and then I fainted. I don't know how long I remained unconscious, but after some time, I came to. And knowing that there were still a lot of residents in the villages around, I started moving in that direction. And in the morning hours, I saw convoys of refugees, not knowing who they are. But among them, I recognised a man and I approached him. And he helped me. I had a lot of wounds, a lot of swellings on my face. I had burns. These people took care of me. They treated my wounds. I spent some time there and then they transferred me to the liberated territory. I met up with my family there, continued treatment, and then after that went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were killed at Ratine?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: On the truck, there were 24 people together with me, and then when we add that another man, then that means 25. I managed to escape, and that means that 24 people were killed. In mid-1999, they exhumed the area around that stable and they managed to identify six bodies. They found a lot of bullet casings. They found wire used to tie hands, and also remains of those younger men who were throwing bodies in. So that means that there were 24 people who were burned there and killed. I don't know whether the OTP wants me to describe what happened between the 1st and the 5th. Would you like me to describe that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. Thank you. That's in your statements. Can I ask you: Of the men killed at Ratine, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of those who shot the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms, if any, were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms, and those people were led by Pero Elez and Zeko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many men were detained with you while you were in the gunpowder magazine?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: There were 85 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many of those 85 men are alive today?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Nothing is known about them. I think that I'm the only one who survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to ask you a few general questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, it is -- if you think you could finish in two minutes, fine, but if not, then perhaps we should first have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think it would be best to have a break, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness. We'll have a break for 25 minutes. But, as I indicated earlier to you, it could be longer for you because we still have to hear the testimony of another witness. So I assume that we'll resume later this morning, which would be in approximately, I would say in approximately two hours, then, it would be from now. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. And I'd like to turn into private session just for a very brief moment before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just before the break, in private session, I invited the parties to see whether an agreement can be reached in terms of time. If there's any information about that, I'd like to turn into private session and hear that information. If there's no information, we don't have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suggest we go into private session, Your Honour. We do have some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then go for just one or two minutes into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's confirmed on our screen now that we are in open session. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did indicate to -- I indicated to Mr. Hannis a few minutes ago, we had a discussion that we would have a distinct preference, if there is to be a five-day break, reserving our position on everything else, Your Honour, we would have a distinct preference for the same week that the Prosecution would prefer. But if the difficulties are insurmountable, well the problem with insurmountable difficulties is you can't surmount them. But we -- and this is not the application which we've been talking about, but, Your Honour, immediately we do make the practical suggestion, we wonder whether the Trial Chamber would consider breaking for both those weeks, just on the basis that it is absolutely clear, we suggest, that that would be helpful in all sorts of ways. So we wonder whether the Trial Chamber would consider simply a two-week break, regardless of everything else we have to sort out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then I think we have interrupted the examination-in-chief of Mr. Hadzic, and is there any -- has the matter been resolved as far as attachments are concerned in relation to the previous witness, whose cross-examination has not yet been concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Margetts answers that question, we had a proposal. Mr. Gaynor indicates he only has 10 or 15 minutes to go to complete his direct exam of the witness he was working on and we propose to do that and then resume with the other witness. That would give Ms. Loukas additional time to prepare for cross-exam and we would have a logical breaking point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that agreeable for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It has the drawback that it's going to carry us over the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of your indication of yesterday, the cross-examination will be concluded anyhow today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's only Your Honour means that I've been here all morning in the circumstances. But all right. Never mind. We live with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Stewart. The other witness has now been informed that he has to wait for two hours. We then have to explain again why he would come back immediately. It would take Mr. Stewart to be in court for two sessions, where we had more or less arranged that he would be there only for one. So the Chamber would prefer to resume the cross-examination of the previous witness, which is Mr. Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm very grateful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, as there is a moment while the witness is being fetched, may I just raise a couple of matters to use up the time. One is this, Your Honour, that we delivered to the United Nations Detention Unit last Friday a CD in relation to witness 608. There's no mystery about Witness 608. In fact, this is the current witness, Mr. Dzambasovic. Your Honour, it's not been delivered to Mr. Krajisnik yet. It's -- I've made inquiries -- we've made follow-up inquiries. I inquired of the unit yesterday to the deputy superintendent and I made a further inquiry in the last half-hour. We don't know what happens but it appears that one week later, almost, we're coming up to Friday afternoon, material that we delivered for Mr. Krajisnik hasn't got to him. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll instruct the Registry to inquire into the matter and to see. So whatever information you have, please give it -- about dates of delivery, what it was, et cetera, and the Registry will -- well, will give us the relevant information. So therefore, full notice is taken of your observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We get all sorts of very helpful cooperation from the UNDU, but occasionally we have these quite serious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You see there's no hesitation. It should be inquired into.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I also mention. I asked Mr. Harmon by e-mail overnight sometime first thing this morning -- frankly, I'm afraid I can't remember whether it's late last night or first thing this morning, they tend to merge together sometimes. But I asked him about an exhibit list in relation to next Monday's witness, Mr. Kljuic. That's 526. He said he'd let me have it when he got it and when he decided. But I would like to observe, we don't have a preliminary list at the moment and with a witness such as him, where there is potentially large amounts of material, we must, please, have an indication. It's Friday and the witness is coming up on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that immediate attention is given to the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Dzambasovic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and the Defence counsel will now resume the cross-examination. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, Your Honour. In my attempt to get the microphone suitably near I've eliminated the transcript from the screen. We'll just sort that out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, good morning. In your statement signed in October 2002, that's the longer statement, this is at page 4, there's a paragraph, you say: "As to who participated in this effort to block mobilisation, I recall that the people doing this were part of the SDS and SDA organisations in the municipalities. Also, I recall that all legal authorities in the municipalities obstructed mobilisation." Can you say what you mean by the phrase "all legal authorities in the municipalities"? It's the "all legal authorities" phrase I'm specifically asking about.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, for the first time in history, in the history of the former JNA, what happened was that the civilian authorities and the organs of MUP were obstructing the mobilisation process. Up until that time, all the mobilisation calls that were carried out enjoyed the full support of the organs of power and authority, regardless of what it was about. But at the time, we had the parties, the newly established parties after the multi-party elections, coming to the fore and taking centre stage, and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond instead of lending support, what happened was that there was obstruction with respect to all aspects of mobilisation, from the official authorities, the municipalities from which our brigade was to be mobilised, et cetera. This was a precedent, and it was because of the problems that ensued and the problems we had that we informed the superior command of the 4th Corps in Sarajevo and the command of the 4th Corps in Sarajevo informed the superior command in Belgrade, in turn. We didn't know what was actually going on and what was happening, and for us soldiers, professional soldiers, this took us by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Later on in your statement, and this is at page 9, there's a paragraph towards the bottom of that page, in English it begins: "Things only became worse as time went on regarding the illegal removal of JNA and TO weapons." Then you refer to chaos. And you say: "However, it's my professional opinion that the removal was not done in an atmosphere of chaos; rather, it was very well planned and organised by senior Serb political and military officials." Now, that's your assessment, Mr. Dzambasovic. But is the -- isn't this the position: You actually don't know yourself of any particular senior Serb political officials who were involved in that planning and organisation, do you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't quite like that. At the time, that is to say during that period, I did not officially know that this was organised from the highest -- by the highest military leadership and political leadership. Later on, I saw the documents for myself. So this assessment on my part, I confirmed -- was confirmed by the documents I saw later on. I don't know if you have the documents. I myself saw them. And I think the investigators that I talked to also saw those documents. So officially speaking, the military peaks, on the basis of the decision made by the political leadership, wrote out an order, the corresponding order, to the effect that all weapons and equipment and materiel from the centres where the Muslims and Croats were in the majority should be dislocated, should be moved. And there are official documents to bear that out. As I say, at that time, during that particular period of time, that is to say, 1991 and 1992, I didn't actually see those documents, nor did I know of their existence. Later on, I learnt of their existence and I actually saw the documents myself. But that's what actually happened in practice It really did take place. So the implementation of the orders that were given and the documents, on the basis of those documents, took place in 1991 and 1992. And there are official documents to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, can we establish one thing. It seems clear, in fact it's clear from especially from a paragraph which has come out of your statement, nevertheless the point arises: Since the actual events in the early 1990s, you have done a considerable amount of work and had a considerable amount of discussion with others and have done a considerable amount of research into documentation in relation to these events of 1991 and 1992, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when I say "considerable," it's an elastic term, but really a lot? That's right, isn't it? By any standards, a great deal of work?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on the professional analyses of those documents, the official documents, in relation to what I saw in practice, myself, and in relation to matters that I was eyewitness to. I was eyewitness to the events and activities. And also from what I had heard from my colleagues, whether from my superior command or from my own level. So all this was done taking into account all those various elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the answer to my question is yes, isn't it, by any standards, a great deal of work?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that the answer is in the affirmative, in a way. That is to say, I did have occasion and I was asked by the powers that be, by the Tribunal and my own defence ministry, to work on documents of that kind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, you're engaged, employed, at the moment, aren't you, as an investigator in another case before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that is a case where the defendant --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it one defendant, Mr. Halilovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got enough to deal with this case without going deeply into that case as well, Mr. Dzambasovic, but in a nutshell, how long have you been employed as an investigator in relation to that case? By the way, you're a Defence team investigator, aren't you, in that case?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since September -- the 26th of September, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you subject to the counsel, legal team, but are you effectively in charge of the defence investigation in that case?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked by the Registry of the Tribunal. I was appointed officially as an investigator in the defence team for Sefer Halilovic, and that mandate started from September last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. All I'm asking is in practical terms, of course you're assigned that way, but for practical purposes, you are the lead investigator; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the lawyers I work with think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's not spend a huge amount of time on that, Mr. Dzambasovic. In two sentences, what's that case about?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that case is linked to the events of 1993 in the Neretva River Valley. They're linked to Grabovica and Uzdol, that is to say, villages with a majority Croat population where, based on the indictment, a crime had taken place and where it did in fact take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Sefer Halilovic, your client, again, in a sentence or two sentences perhaps at the maximum, who is and was he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in that specific case, for that period relevant to the indictment, he was the chief of the Main Staff and the commander was someone else. He was General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
