utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzambasovic, I should in fairness make it clear, this is not in any way an attack on you, this next question, but it is a fair summary, isn't it, to say that although there are things which you obviously say you saw yourself firsthand, and it's clear in many cases from your statement what you say you actually saw, you were there, but otherwise, when you are expressing views about what happened in 1991 and 1992, by this time your views are a synthesis of what you saw and all the very considerable amount of work which you have done since with others over a number of years? That's a fair summary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't think you're attacking me, and of course you couldn't attack me for what I wrote in the statement. Because they are events and activities whose witness I was. So there's no personality or any person -- even if Mr. Milosevic were here, I'm sure he would confirm all my observations and statements, because they are authentic, both the events and the allegations and observations. But of course my opinions with respect to what I saw at the time there or what I experienced at the time and heard at the time, have been coupled and borne out by the documents and analyses that I conducted later on. That's absolutely correct too. Or rather, they just serve to confirm what I saw myself, what I heard and experienced at the time myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, in your statement at page 11, you say: "I am providing a document, document 2. This document is from the Assembly of the Serb people and dated December 1991. It directed the SDS to form Serb organisations and units." Now, I should say, Your Honour, that's a paragraph which it was indicated over the break, it was suggested should be cut out of the statement. And in a sense, I'm happy for it to come out of the statement except for this point, which I raised with Mr. Margetts, which is: Now, witness, that document that you were talking about, dated December 1991, which you described as a document from the Assembly of the Serb People, is the document which is commonly and notoriously known as variants A and B, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzambasovic. Please assume unless I make it clear that anybody else is the person being asked, it will be you. You're the witness.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document and several others dating back to 1991, so one of them I saw in 1991, actually, because for some reason, I don't know if you've got it, but my colleague Major Krstovic was appointed Minister of Defence of the SAO Krajina or the SAO, Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija. I was surprised by that and then later on I saw the documents themselves. Some of them I saw earlier, some later. But where my colleague was appointed minister of defence, I saw while I was still in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that document -- and I'm happy for the Prosecution to assist on this if it would speed things up. But, Mr. Dzambasovic, is that document that you refer to there in your statement, is that the document which is commonly known as variants A and B or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, should we -- if it would be that document, I don't know whether you're seeking confirmation or denial of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's -- confirmation would be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, but I'll deal with whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is document 2 referred to on page 11, I think it is, is that what is known here and what is already in evidence the document -- the A and B variation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is difficult for the witness, obviously, to answer without the statement and the attachments there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Parties agree that reference is made here to the Variant A and B document of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy. I did indicate to Mr. Margetts over the break and he very helpfully agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason I have to ask it in that way, Mr. Dzambasovic, is because you do then later on in your statement in a passage which remains in that statement, you do bring up the question of variants A and B. So, Your Honour, I wonder if the witness could, therefore, be handed -- it's P66. Your Honour is quite right. It's long been in evidence and it's P66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you find P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then they told me it isn't, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No wonder I was confused. It's P65, but it is in binder 6 - I think it's Mr. Treanor's binder - binder 6, document 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you get all these 6s, it's a devil of a job to keep the documents straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the B/C/S version will be presented to the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it is helpful if the witness has his statement for these purposes, Your Honour. I'm talking about the longer statement, October 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have that already? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I mean his B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can carry on a little bit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you've been handed the Variant A and B document already, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was handed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, the first point is this and I believe I'm entitled to ask this question even though the paragraph is supposedly coming out of your statement. In your statement you describe this document as a document from the Assembly of the Serb People. Now, would you agree, that's clearly not right, or at least -- well, let's take it in stages. There is nothing on the document itself to indicate that it came from the Assembly of the Serb People, is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dzambasovic, I see that you're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suspect His Honour was just interested, Mr. Dzambasovic, in whether it was just sandwiches you were getting out of your suitcase or briefcase or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said he was looking for a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no sandwiches in my bag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I instruct you not to write on any document that is in evidence, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not going to write anything. Let me just inspect this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I was putting to you that there is -- in the first place, there is nothing on that document itself to indicate that it came from the Assembly of the Serb People, and I'm inviting your agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what is stated here, this is the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is the party Main Board. Perhaps in the statement, I said Assembly, or wrote Assembly, because the Assembly is mentioned frequently in the text, to the effect that the Assembly is to pass a decision and so on. But it's not a contentious issue. You can see who authored the document, on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, in effect, you've answered my next question, which is that your -- what you say about the source of this document is entirely gained from the content of the document itself. And from nowhere else?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You refer in your statement -- do you have your statement now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I don't know what page it is in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But around halfway through, there's a passage where you list 23 items. It's not what we specifically want to look at; it's just so that we can find the place. Do you see there's a page or so where you list 23 numbered items, assignments? Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And then just two or three paragraphs down from that, you refer to your diary, and then you talk about -- you say: "As to one item, people should decide against using their holidays," and then you make a note in your diary, and then you say you remember item 10 in the SDS Serb Variant A and B plan states organise and inform all Serbian personnel not to use their holidays in the coming period and not to travel. And you say that you remember that item being briefed by Colonel Milosevic. And then you say: "Next you can see the item 11 specifies which units should be brought up to JNA standards, manpower for wartime strengths. And do you have in mind there, if we look at item 11 in the document, it's Variant A in English, first level, and then we've got a number of items. It says: "11. Preparations are to be made. Organisational and other conditions created for ..." And then the second dashed item is: "Reinforcing war units according to the specialties in the JNA." That's what you have in mind when you talk in your statement about which units should be brought up to JNA standards, is it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify that. So these 23 assignments in my statement were the original assignments conveyed to us by Commander Milosevic, which he, in turn, received from General Kukanjac, commander of the 2nd Military District. And then let us now compare these assignments with the assignments mentioned in the statement. So these are original assignments which we received from the commander of the 2nd Military District. And if we compare these assignments to this document that you gave me concerning the instructions on organising the Serbian people and so on, this is how I came to the conclusion which I gave in the statement, which means that these two are in accordance, meaning that political decisions of the Serbian people were implemented in the army through the adequate orders of the military commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was asking you specifically about item 11. In your statement, you say that item 11 -- can we agree on this: When you talk about item 11 in your statement, you are meaning to talk about item 11 in this Variant A and B document, are you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my statement, item 11 does not correspond to the other one, to the item 11 in the other document. In my statement -- let me just take a look which item pertains to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, can I help, please. Just -- I hope I will try and get to the point here and indicate --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. -- Why I want to get this clear. In your statement, you say, as to one item, people should decide against using their holidays, your diary, page 55, item 12, you say: "I remember item 10 in Variant A and B. I clearly remember this item being briefed by Colonel Milosevic. Next you can see that item 11 specifies which units." Now, on a simple reading, Witness, the problem is that it's not at all clear then, having referred to an item in your diary and an item in Variant A and B, we are then left a little bit in the dark when you refer to a numbered item as to which document you're talking about. So that's why I have to ask you there whether, when you talk about item 11, you are talking about item 11 in the document Variant A and B or talking about item 11 in the list in your diary. Now, do you need to have your diary put in front of you for this purpose? I suspect you probably do now.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diary is one of the exhibits that we'll be presenting to the Court, so we could distribute that to the Court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that it has been distributed already. It's among the documents that were given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. There's a batch of stuff. And I have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that document could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, these were attachments to the statement. The statements have not received exhibit numbers up until now. So if you would not mind, I would rather deal with all the documents in its context. But we all know now that we are looking at the diary of this witness, which has not yet been granted -- attributed a number but which looks like this in the original version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed and we'll deal with the numbering at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I don't know what's the perfect way to deal with this issue in future, but I think our experience here indicates that it isn't the way we've all been dealing with it. We're going to have to think about this a bit for the future. But never mind today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you have your diary. Your page numbering will be different, but the dates will be the same, we trust. This is at page 19 of 38 in the English printout, but I think it's page 54. But any way, it's 5th of February, 1992 in your own Serbian diary. You're there at that page, are you, with 24 -- it's at least 24, the 24 numbered items that appear under the heading of: "Tasks of the commander of the 2nd Military District." Are we at the same page, point?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I've found it. I've found it in the original. And I see that in the statement, there are some things that have not been translated. Item 2, it says: "Unintelligible." The next item says: "Prevent provocations and be prepared for a decisive attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were interested in the item pertaining to leaves, annual leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It looks as if -- has the numbering -- I don't -- well, I don't think it has, actually. Item 12 is dealing with annual leave, but actually, although I'm very interested in that, Mr. Dzambasovic, I'm more interested even in that point where you refer to item 11, and I just want to be clear. We're going back to where we were now. You've got the documents. In your statement, when you refer -- you say you see that item 11 specifies which units should be brought up to JNA standards, manpower for wartime strengths. Are you talking about an item in the various A and B document or are you talking about an item in your diary? That's the simple starting point for the question.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a simple item. So these 23 assignments listed in my diary are the assignments received from the commander of the 2nd Military District. They have nothing to do with the documents which you have shown to me, the instruction of the Main Board of the SDS. So these 23 assignments have nothing to do with this instruction issued by the Main Board of the SDS. These are the assignments given to the subordinates by the commander of the 2nd Military District, issued to his subordinates and subordinated units. But only upon analysing these assignments can you reach the conclusion that these are in accordance with the political decisions of the Serbian people. So what I stated earlier, that the implementation of political decisions of the Serbian people was practically implemented through the army, through commands and orders issued to the relevant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, so to try and distil the essence of that: You are saying that here in your statement, you have engaged in, in effect, a retrospective matching of the Variant A and B document against the briefing that you received in February 1992 to identify where they correspond in substance? Is that a fair distillation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. It is partially so. What I explained to you earlier, I said as follows: I was an authentic witness. I was there. I saw and I heard. Some of it I confirmed, I was able to confirm through the documents that I saw later. And it is possible that in the future I will come across some other documents that I haven't seen so far. And based on that, perhaps I would be able to come up with other details. But your statement is correct about what you just asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just specifically, then, in that matching process, I do want to just dwell on item 11 for a moment longer, please. You say in your statement that item 11 specifies which units should be brought up to JNA standards. So please, can you point out where in either of the documents that you have in front of you, or indeed a general invitation to any other document, where it specifies which units should be brought up to JNA standards.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you are not a soldier, and all units should have been Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond brought up to the standard. There was no exception there. Our main task, our main focus, was always to establish combat readiness, in accordance with the standards, and that pertained to all commands and to all units, without exception. That was the most important task we had, to raise combat readiness of a unit, which means to prepare the unit so that it can carry out a combat assignment. With respect to all of the elements, training, logistics, tactics, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're right, I'm not a soldier, Mr. Dzambasovic. But what I'm inviting us all to do here in a legal environment is to stick to the question and answer the question, please, Mr. Dzambasovic. I'm asking you where in anything which could be regarded as an item 11, where you say it specifies which -- specifies, it's got to say it in writing, Mr. Dzambasovic. Where does it say that, which units should be brought up to JNA standards? It's not a military question really, Mr. Dzambasovic. Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here in the assignment, under item 5, just an illustration, the reinforcement of war units in accordance with realistic possibilities. And this is what I just told you about. There are many examples of this nature, but I'm not prepared now -- I wasn't prepared for that question, so I don't have them at my disposal right now. So it says here: Reinforcement of the war units. I put down an abbreviation. RJ stands for war units. In accordance with the realistic possibilities. So that was one of the assignments. And then it says here to decrease the use of mines and explosives and ammunition, and then it says here to secure equipment for units for 45 days, meaning 45 days of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, let's not go through the list unless I specifically ask you. Item 5 on the list, it's item 5 in the English, anyway, "remanning," it's been translated as or "reinforcing the war units according to the realistic possibilities," that is not at all specifying which units should be brought up to JNA standards, is it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is not written here. I've already said to you that you're not going to find it written anywhere that this was the 216th Brigade of the 4th Corps. When the commander of the military district addresses his units, he doesn't list individual units, he just says it in general and we as soldiers, we know what combat readiness is. It consists of six elements and it is enough for him to say, "raise the level of combat readiness," and we will know what he had in mind. He doesn't have to list individual units, because that order pertains to all units in the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, I'm going to try simply to shorten this issue, because we can all -- and the Trial Chamber can read Variant A and B and the Trial Chamber can read your diary and match or not match. So I'm not going to take everybody's time on exploring it at length. But I want to get this clear from you, then: This Variant A and B document at this time to you, in February 1992, it was unknown to you as a document it didn't come into the picture; it was actually -- you were just unaware of that altogether when you received this briefing from your superior officer? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I did not see this document at the time, but I saw this other document in which my colleague Krstovic was appointed minister of defence of the SAO Romanija. So later, when I see these documents, I was able to see for myself that this was an implementation of political decisions through the assignments issued to the army and implemented by the army on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And some features, without dwelling on it in detail, but a number of features of what we see in Variant A and B, if they -- well, they include just obvious things, don't they, which in any conflict or potential conflict situation as a matter of common sense would have to be done by any military organisation. They're just many of them blindingly obvious, aren't they? For example, protection of material resources, ensuring the continuation of production and services of vital importance for defence. It's just all -- I'm not saying there's anything wrong with it. It's just obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I see many faults here. That is my assessment, and I have already told you about that. Because secret warehouses were not quite proper, because that means that Muslims and Croats should have also had secret warehouses. All people should have had them. And in one of the items of that document, it says establish secret warehouses. So this is not a normal assignment, a normal situation. All of the nations should have had these secret warehouses, not just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The documents that you referred to generally a little while ago as showing you that the removal of JNA and TO weapons and ammunitions was very well planned and organised by senior Serb political and military officials, and concentrating on political officials: Can you point to or identify a document which shows a senior Serb political official being involved in the planning and organisation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically that the document was such-and-such, but it is absolutely true that the Assembly of the Serb People, as the highest political organ, did make decisions of that nature, like this set of instructions referring to warehouses and depots, and in actual fact, everything that was decided politically was put into practice in the army through the orders of the top officials of the federal secretariat for national defence in Belgrade, starting at the top there, and then down the chain, towards the lower units. And that's absolutely true. I don't think anybody challenges that. Everybody will be able to tell you the same thing. That line, that chain, was established and implemented in that way. The political organs would make the decisions, the federal secretary would turn that into an order, the political ruling into an order, and the order would be sent down from the top levels to the lowest level of units and their commands, down the chain of command. That's the usual chain and all the links in the chain. So it's not anything that one would challenge. All politicians and soldiers would bear that out and tell you that that was the way things worked. That was the customary system according to which the whole system worked, functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear, Mr. Dzambasovic: You're saying then, are you, that so far as the involvement of senior Serb political officials in this planning and organisation is concerned, that your knowledge of documentary support for that is effectively public knowledge. The documents that you're referring to are the publicly available documents, such as minutes, reports of decisions of the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So that was public, they were public documents, and it is on that basis that I say that they follow the military orders. I did of course have the military orders. I saw those military orders. And they were all formulated on the basis of the political decisions. So I myself did not have any practical links with politicians, nor did I have any dealings with them, because, as a professional soldier, that wasn't my duty, it wasn't within my job description at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a point -- it's a self-contained point. You say in your -- this longer statement that as to payment of volunteer soldiers, "payment was not the practice before 1991 to 1992." And then you say: "Now", you're talking about that period then, late 1991, early 1991: "Those soldiers that responded to mobilisation were being paid." Now, just let me put this to you: In another statement - and we needn't go back to it, because the question will be clear - you had indicated that once reservists had been called up, they were treated exactly the same. Is there a distinction you're drawing here between reservists who were called up and volunteer soldiers? Can you reconcile the two? Do you see what I'm saying? You indicated in an earlier statement that once people had been called up, then they were all treated exactly the same, presumably paid the same. How does this relate to what you're saying, that payment of some soldiers before 1991, 1992, was not the practice?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's an admirably short answer, Mr. Dzambasovic, in a situation where I wouldn't mind a longer one. Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite clear on that, and I'll explain it to you simply. In practice, up until then, up until 1991, all those who responded to the call for mobilisation, the call-up, would receive remuneration in their companies, in the companies they worked for. It was called a refund. So the company, the firm they worked in, would, in an organised manner, send a list to the military command, a list of the employees from that particular firm who were called up on the basis of a mobilisation or for exercise and training, and the army would refund those monies through the firm's organisation or the organisation of the company. So that was standard practice. Now, in 1991 and later on, that is to say, after the first mobilisation and the second mobilisation, that practice was violated, and anybody who responded would be personally paid out his per diems and the money owed him, regardless of whether the person was a member of the unit or not. The essential point was that he had joined up in the unit. Now, where he had come from, who had sent him, that didn't matter. But up until then, that could not have happened. So in the second variant, they were paid on the spot by the army, regardless of whether they were within the frameworks of that unit or not. So somebody could have come from the moon, for example. He would be paid. And that was not the practice previously, and that's why I stated that. It seems to be contradictory in the statement, but it isn't, because that's what happened and how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You described how TO commanders visited Colonel Milosevic, and you said you tried to remain a professional officer throughout these events. You were waiting for a political solution to be reached. "I don't know what these people were talking about with Milosevic. Only in retrospect can I say it seemed as they were preparing the Serbian side for aggression. The goal was to prepare the condition of the creation of Greater Serbia." When you use the phrase "the creation of Greater Serbia," can you describe what you have in mind in that description?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, as a soldier myself, I worked on the elaboration of war plans for my unit. As the chief of staff, I was the protagonist of the elaboration of those war plans. And we elaborated those war plans and devised them quite legally, in premises which were set aside for that purpose, and they had a certain degree of confidentiality, of secrecy, this elaboration and writing and compiling of war plans. All war plans up until then I had worked on them. I was a participant working on the writing of the war plans. One day, and you'll find this in my diary, you'll have the date there, Colonel Milosevic, the then-colonel - he's a general now - explained that there were some new war plans. Now, I became worried. How could there be new war plans when I should be working on them? So nobody could bypass the Chief of Staff there. But as I say new war plans were compiled and written without the participation of the officers who were not Serbs. So no non-Serbs could take part in the elaboration of those new war plans. The new war plans themselves contained elements which coincided -- we can't say that they were identical, but they coincided with the borders of a Greater Serbia, greatly. 90 per cent. They coincided 90 per cent with the borders of a Greater Serbia and they contained combat activities and actions to go out and take positions at those borders. So those war plans were compiled without the participation of the soldiers, the officers who were not Serb officers. It was only the Serbs, exclusively Serb soldiers and officers worked on the compiling of those plans. So that was that variation. All the other officers were excluded from the process. We didn't even know about it until that particular day when Colonel -- the colonel reported to us and said that there were new war plans. So it was impossible for plans of that kind to have been devised, because they are very unwieldy documents, they are documents contained in ten files, ten binders, comprising the complete, entire war plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, what do you mean by "Greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in theory and practice, there is a map of that Greater Serbia. I think you have the map. It is common knowledge. It is well known. So that implies, and I imply the territory in which the Serb people were expected to live, following that theory of -- the theory that was developed in the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in Belgrade and which was publicly talked about in those days and during those years not only in Bosnia but in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, saying that the Serbs wanted to live in one state, that that would be the territory of a Greater Serbia and that the borders and frontiers of that state would be Virovitica, Karlovac, Karlobag, roughly speaking, that kind of line, that kind of frontier and border. It doesn't matter whether I've left out some particular place on that line. But that is what we had to work with. In that piece of information that was given to us publicly and that we heard about talked about very frequently and that's why I said that they were planning to set up that kind of territory, which according to that theory would belong to a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in your statement, and this is at page 27 of the English version, you say: "As to why the army reorganised, the Serb senior leaders did this to make sure that the republics did not have authority and responsibility over the army on their soil." So when you talk there about the Serb senior leaders, you're talking about people in Serbia, in Belgrade, are you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the military leadership and Serb leadership in general in the former Yugoslavia. When the reorganisation of the army took place in 1988, the reorganisation I've already spoken about, we as soldiers were informed about that and we all supported it, in declarative terms, of course, because the explanations we were given seemed to us to be normal. Instead of having seven military districts, four military districts were set out. The command was reduced. The army was being rationalised. So if somebody were to present you something in that way, of course you would say, and the times were such, that everything that went towards rationalisation you thought was better, which means that the number of links and chains were reduced, the commands were reduced, and so on. So nobody gave much thought to the fact that this had some other objectives, that there were some other objectives behind it. So very few people even theoretically, that it occurred to anybody even theoretically that there were other objectives. But what happened in practice in 1991 and 1992 confirms this all. The military districts were done away with, the Territorial Defence was done away with in the republics, to stop the political leadership of the republic to command units of the Territorial Defence. Because following the constitution, this came under the competence of the republics and provinces. So with this new reorganisation, this was done away with. This competence of theirs was taken away from them, and of course that was an afterthought or intelligence after hindsight, based on what came to pass later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time, in 1991 and early 1992, at the time, you had no knowledge of any involvement of Serb senior leaders in any of this process, did you, well, apart from anything that you could publicly read and hear in the same way that anybody else could? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is right. The federal secretary, and I have to explain it to you, the federal secretary, Veljko Kadijevic, in 1993, wrote a very nice book in which he set out everything that we experienced, saw, lived through, or thought might be the reason. And he confirms that in 1993, when he wrote his book entitled: "My vision of the dismantling of Yugoslavia." Disintegration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, if one day Mr. Kadijevic or his book turn up to give evidence, it's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. That's why I said it, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: General Dzambasovic, you were asked about the Variant A and B document, and the question was, in relation to the content of that document, and it was stated to you that it included just obvious things, which in any conflict or potential conflict situation, as a matter of common sense, would have to be done by any military organisation. Was it normal for political parties to produce documents such as Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not customary, nor was this the job of the organs of power and authority ever. And if you will recall, I mentioned yesterday that they were precedents and were major blows to us and took us completely by surprise when we saw that the organs of power and authority in politics had meddled in something that would never occur to you could come under their competence and authority, because the army or rather the ministry, the Ministry of Defence would always see to matters of that kind and that was a first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: General Dzambasovic, you were asked whether you could point to a document that shows a senior political figure involved in planning and organisation. Did the document Variant A and B refer to the involvement of the senior organ of the SDS party in planning and organisation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Main Board of the SDS is mentioned. Now, as to hierarchy, the hierarchy of the SDS, I don't want to go into that, but the Main Board of the SDS means Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't a local community. It wasn't the municipality. It was the top level at the Bosnia-Herzegovina level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You were asked whether your information in relation to the involvement of political figures in planning and organisation was restricted to public documents. Was Variant A and B a public document in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, don't really see how that question can really reasonably be asked because the witness has made it quite clear that he did not himself see that document, so the question simply doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts. Isn't it true that the questions by the Defence were about the knowledge of the witness at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You were asked about the formation of Greater Serbia, and you stated that the war plans that you subsequently learnt of approximated the plan to form Greater Serbia to approximately 90 per cent. To what extent did these war plans correspond with what was eventually to become Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: These war plans, the ones that were compiled at top level - I don't know if you have them - but they did coincide, for the most part, with the borders of the so-called Greater Serbia. At lower levels, lower down, that is to say, from that top level, the war plans were also devised lower down the chain. Now, how far they coincided with the territory of Republika Srpska in concrete terms, I really can't say. I don't know. I didn't see the plans myself, the plans for all these units. I didn't have access to those plans, so I really can't say specifically and answer your question. However, in practice, what was done in practical terms in 1991, in the preparations to war, can be assessed and evaluated on the basis of the positions set up in 1991, by where the artillery was located, where the tanks were located, and so on and so forth, what it looked like. You can gain a picture of what it looked like on the basis of that and that is the only way I can base my conclusions or assessments, but I don't think I can do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You were asked about your knowledge of the involvement of Serb senior leaders in this planning and organisation. Was Rajko Dukic involved?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic did take part in that, and I had occasion, or rather, all the municipal leaderships met -- I met them many times, from the Rogatica, Sokolac, Olovo, Han Pijesak municipalities, Vlasenica municipality, and in my statement, I think I give the names that I happen to remember, people that delved in politics, people who worked in the municipal organs of the Territorial Defence, and those who worked in the SDS as well. So from those municipalities. I saw those people on a number of occasions. They would come many times. And what I stress, which is an absurdity, if you ask me, once again, was that -- and it was so absurd, in actual fact, that the political power and those organs of political power had taken over all the army's functions and we were practically left without the most normal functions. They would meddle in everything, at all levels, the political powers that be. That was a situation that was not tenable. It was completely absurd. And even in the documents I showed you, you can see, precisely defined, what it says. It doesn't say JNA units. It says SDS units, from the Commander of the 2nd Military District Kukanjac down the line. So this was done by the organs of power and authority, and that was the absurdity that happened and that had never happened before to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Judge El Mahdi has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to seek clarification from you on one point, and it concerns the two appeals for mobilisation, the two call-ups for mobilisation. The first was dated the 30th of June, I believe, 1991; and the second mobilisation call came in September. Now, you say that the two political parties reacted in the sense that when the people responded to the first call-up, and you quoted the two parties, the SDS and the SDA, however, you also said that with respect to the second mobilisation call, which came approximately one month after the first mobilisation, that the people who responded to the mobilisation call were Serbs in the majority. The overwhelming majority were Serbs. Now, to your knowledge, and you have -- do you have an answer to that? Was it that the party had changed? Was it that the Serbs who responded were responding, in fact, to directives? Or was it a general response to the mobilisation call, that all citizens should respond? What would you say? What was the reason for that overwhelming Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that question. It's a very good one. Your observation is quite true. For the first time, the political -- both political parties in power tried to obstruct the mobilisation call, and that is absolutely correct and true and it is not in dispute. Now, what happened when the second mobilisation was called up? For the second mobilisation, there was a turning point that took place in the former JNA. On that occasion, the JNA, in all practical terms, became the army of just one ethnic group, and that was the Serb ethnic group, the Serb nationality. And I have to refer back once again, although I didn't know that at the time, to the fact that the army, to all intents and purposes, had become the army of just one ethnic groups, the Serbs, and once again Veljko Kadijevic says this in his books. He says in practical terms the JNA surrendered on the 31st of July, 1991. I think that's what he says in his books. Which means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. My question was quite precise. Do you know the attitude of the parties, that the SDS party took, specifically speaking, with respect to the mobilisation and to that matter?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, in concrete terms, up until then, that is to say, during the first mobilisation, the attitude of the SDS was not Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond defined when it came to the army. They had no definite position. When it came to the second mobilisation, the SDS did have a clear-cut stand towards the army, and all -- everybody endeavoured to have as many people respond as possible. And this was different to the first mobilisation, because the second time round, the weapons distribution had started, the units were being displaced and moved, as was ammunition and equipment to places with a Serb majority. So the SDS joined the army, joined up with the army, and that is why in the second mobilisation it was only the Serbs who responded in such an overwhelming majority, and that's why the units became mono-ethnic, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the information that you've been giving us, where were you able to learn about that and to gain your opinions? Do you have any tangible arguments to bear that out, to support your claims?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do, and that is why, because it was such a sensitive question I complained twice to the commander of the 4th Corps, for instance, my superior command, General Djurdjevac, what was being done in practice. Each unit has its own position and place in the mobilisation near the barracks, and it is usually 10 to 12 square kilometres in area. Now what was happening was something quite abnormal. Instead of having a mobilisation in Han Pijesak, what happened was that the mobilising took place in Rogatica, Sokolovic [phoen] and Milici, under the auspices and leadership of the leaders of the SDS in actual facts, the activists as they called themselves. And I saw all that with my own eyes. Don't you think it was absurd? I myself was not able to attend the establishment of a unit and in my own municipality, that of Rogatica, for example, I could not see what was going on. I didn't have access to what was going on, for instance. That was quite absurd. So this is something that I experienced myself and saw for myself. And now the SDS officials, whom I know to this day, could not say anything other than what I have told you. They would not be able to assert anything different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you at this moment. Is there any need to put further questions to the witness, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just a tiny point to clear up, because His Honour Judge El Mahdi asked about the mobilisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you give just ever-so-slightly different dates in relation to the first mobilisation. You say in an earlier statement that it was the 29th of June and then in a later statement you say it was the 30th of July and Judge El Mahdi, perhaps understandably, synthesised those and said it was the 30th of June. Which date is it? You seem to have knowledge of specific dates. Can we just get the date clear.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can check the date out. It was a Saturday. Now, whether it was the 29th or 30th of June, don't hold me to the exact date. But it was a Saturday. I know that for sure, because I went off on holiday. It was the first day of my leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was the end of June.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wasn't able actually to go on holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was the end of June rather than the end of July?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 31st of July, I mentioned that in my answer to His Honour the Judge, I said that on the 31st of July, Veljko Kadijevic in his book wrote that to all intents and purposes the army had surrendered. Perhaps you mixed those two up, otherwise mobilisation was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic all it was to get the date straight. You say it was the end of June rather than the end of July, and it was a Saturday. It will probably turn out that the date that Judge El Mahdi put to you is that Saturday, so --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would have one further question in that respect. All the events that you describe, well, let's say on pages 10, 11, that is, the involvement of the SDS in creating special formations, et cetera, that was all after the September mobilisation, call for mobilisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly. 90 per cent of those activities. There were some activities that went on before, but the obvious ones and the ones that I saw myself and experienced myself took place after the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Milici, that's the empowerment of Mr. Dukic, that's the -- these events, that's all after I think at a certain moment you referred to March.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a point of information, the 29th of June was a Saturday. Ms. Cmeric tells me that and I'm certainly not going to argue with her on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually go to holiday on a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not unknown, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzambasovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague. And I heard that you have other activities as well, but if you return home, I wish you a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and my greetings to one and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00, and then we'll resume the examination of the witness we started with. Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter in respect of the 92 bis package. We need to move for the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do that now, before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, about the bundle: I do understand that some kind of an agreement exists between the parties on what parts are still in the statements, what parts are not in the statements. Of course we have not been fully informed about that, but the Chamber would really prefer to receive that material in such a way that we don't have to search for the whole of the transcript to see what part of written statements are in evidence, what parts are not. So if you could prepare that and then we'll deal with the attachments to that at the same time so that we have it all together in its context. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are prepared in regard to that. Counsel and I have agreed on what paragraphs will be excised from the statement, so we're in a position to proceed now if you'd like us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Chamber would like to receive those statements amended according to you, because otherwise we have the statements, we read them, and of course we do not always have in the back of our mind that at a certain day someone said that we should not read paragraph 6. So we'd like to receive that material. Perhaps a version in one language would do; we usually do not read the B/C/S version. So if that would be done on the English version, indication of what is taken out and what is still there, that would be of sufficient guidance for the Chamber. But I do not know whether that would be agreeable for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly endorse, with respect, Your Honour's suggestion. The echo has come back. We shall prepare, agree a marked-up final version. But we do suggest, Your Honour, that it would be appropriate for the extra work to be done to make sure the two language versions match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Perhaps that is better. I'm just aware of what work it takes to prepare that. But we really want to prevent a situation where we are reading materials, not knowing exactly what is in and what is not in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say I'm not proposing to come back and I appreciate the timing this morning enabling me to escape the last session. It's not going to be a holiday, but at least I can be somewhere else. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, how many mosques were there in Kalinovik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four. Three were used and one was not used before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were any of those mosques damaged or destroyed in any way?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, no. During the war, all of them were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you name those mosques which were destroyed, please.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in Jelasica village was destroyed, in Ulog, in Hotovle, and in Kutina from the village where Ratko Mladic is from.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you personally witness the destruction of those mosques?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I heard from the residents of those villages who used to come over. Later, after the war, I was able to see it for myself as well.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence this morning, you spoke about a meeting on the 5th of May, 1992, attended by Grujo Lalovic, at which he gave an assurance that the Muslims of Kalinovik would be protected, their lives and their property would be protected. You went on to say, and in your statements, you said that the Muslims were subjected to imprisonment, killings, and their property was burnt. Why did you trust Grujo Lalovic's assurance that you and your property would not be harmed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, at the time, when we met with Grujo Lalovic, no property was damaged or destroyed. All of that started happening later on, in late May/early June. And I was reminiscing about these events, and I remembered that I had another meeting with Lalovic and Colonel Bundalo, and they invited to the Municipal Assembly building representatives of all Muslim villages where they discussed how to organise life. The commander of the town and president of the Executive Council gave us guarantees to the effect that nothing would happen to us, and then after that there was another meeting with Ratko Bundalo in the village and another meeting with the representatives of the neighbouring Serbian village. All guarantees were given there to us, to the effect that nothing would happen to us or to our property. This is why we decided to remain in our towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you identify the dates on which the subsequent meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember the date, but I know it was in late May, before the conflict started in Trnovo, neighbouring municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, in your statements and in your evidence, you described the arming the Serbs, the disarming of Muslims, the detention of Muslims, the burning of Muslim property, and the killing of Muslim civilians. The first question is this, and please answer with a simple yes or no: Did you form any view as to whether those activities were planned in any way?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what was your view?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kalinovik, we had discussions with the relevant people, with the people in power, who were influential, and at least the way they portrayed it to us was that they received all orders from relevant authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the SAO Trebinje and so on. Because Grujo Lalovic was also a member of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. So my opinion is that all of that had been planned. Ratko Mladic gave guarantees to his neighbours, and he used his authority to remove the guns, and later on, those guns were used again. So that means that somebody was issuing orders for things to happen or for things not to happen. The authorities, the Serbian authorities in Kalinovik, were not kept abreast.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your answer, you said: "In Kalinovik we had discussions with the relevant people, with the people in power who were influential." Could you identify which people you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've referred to Grujo Lalovic, who held the post that I've already enumerated. I also referred to Ratko Bundalo, commander of the town, and also the then-commander of the JNA barracks, Rade Pavlovic. And there were other prominent people, residents of our town. Those were prominent citizens, and they gave us these guarantees.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your previous answer, you also said: "The Serbian authorities in Kalinovik were not kept abreast." What was it that led you to that belief?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one -- they told us one thing, and then in the end something else was implemented. And we think that it was done either because they were not informed or that they purposely tried to portray things one way, where in fact it was actually the other way. They were playing the good cop-bad cop game, one group was protecting us and the other one was beating us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court whether, as a result of your experiences during 1992, you were diagnosed with any form of trauma or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have post-traumatic stress disorder and I still have treatment. My right kidney had to be removed as a result of injuries I received during the war, because it wasn't functional any more.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said your right kidney had to be removed as a result of injuries. What specific injuries are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had injuries from the blows I received on the right side, and after that I always had pain in that area, and I don't know whether this is what caused the kidney to become dysfunctional. But later on it had to be removed. I also have a scar right here on my head. It is a permanent scar. I also had two fingers broken. I have a gunfire wound to my leg. So this is something that will stay as a permanent reminder of the injuries I received, the blows I received. When I do something with my hand, I take a look at my hand and see that my fingers are deformed. So this is a constant reminder of my traumas.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you continue to receive treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm under supervision. I see neuropsychiatrist every two months. My condition is currently stable. I take medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you continue to experience physical pain of any kind as a result of your experiences during 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do experience physical pain. If I just remember 68 people, neighbours, with whom I worked together, with whom I lived, and who are gone now, and another 17 people from Trnovo municipality who are gone as well now, killed in the most atrocious way, so that their remains cannot be found to this day, this is quite enough to remind me of the terrible events I experienced and to create further pain in my soul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, it seems that the witness has not perhaps fully understood the physical pain you were asking him. Could you please clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you experience, apart from the mental suffering which you've described, any physical pain, recurrent physical pain of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the weather is about to change, I have headaches, because I received blows to my head. So this is the kind of physical pain that I have.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Has your post-traumatic stress disorder had any noticeable negative effect on your ability to remember what happened or on your ability to testify about what happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It doesn't have that effect. I never forget what I say, regardless of how I feel mentally, I always have these events before me. Nothing would make me forget that. Nothing would make me diminish the memory of that, especially since I want the truth to triumph. This is my main motive. I want the truth to triumph. The fate of these people, not only the 85 that I've mentioned, but additional 30 that were killed in our village. And when you remember that there was an 18-year-old boy waiting in line for execution with me, and that another 15-year-old was killed with his father, I think that I have to keep it all in mind and always tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we proceed, I will make one point. If there are going to be any more questions in what is basically an area of medical expertise as to whether post-traumatic stress disorder has any noticeable negative effect on your ability to remember, I would submit it's inappropriate to ask any medical, expert medical questions of that nature of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, will there be any further questions on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that you have at the same time drawn the attention of the Chamber to what had happened already.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you have also drawn the attention of the Chamber to the questions already put and already answered by the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I have no further questions of the witness. I have just one minor procedural point which I'll identify now, relating to Exhibit P286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you gave us the wrong map and you want to present another one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's not quite the case. The map is the same. Following the witness's identification on the place of his detention and the place of the execution, the evidence had changed, so a new ERN was given for the map. So the substituted version which the Registrar has bears the new ERN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we had the right one and we get another right one, which is a different one, because this one is in colour. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The difference, Your Honour, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just the ERN number. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's as a result of the witness's identification of A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as a matter of fact, the A and the B are exactly in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. The map without A and B and without the witness's signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- is the original ERN. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's then on the record. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any chance, I'm just asking you, looking at the clock, it's the end of the week, that we could finish by today?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I better put my headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any chance that we could finish by today, do you think? You've still got half on hour. It's Friday, so if that would be possible, it would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can assure the Trial Chamber and the witness that I'm anxious to ensure that we can finish within the half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start and let's see how far we come. Please proceed. You'll now be examined by Ms. Loukas, who is counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, I want to indicate two points to you. Firstly, I don't propose to ask you any questions about the traumatic events you've given evidence of in relation to the detention or the killings, but I'm interested in some of the earlier evidence you gave. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the other aspect is this: I would imagine you're understandably anxious to ensure that you don't have to stay in The Hague for the weekend, and I'm just as anxious to ensure that we finish the cross-examination as soon as possible. So if I ask you a question that you can give a short answer to, if a question is capable of a yes or no, please give a yes or no; if you think it requires explanation, please give that explanation, but try and keep your answers as short as possible so that we can finish within the time allowed this afternoon. Are you with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I do not want to rush. Even though it's Friday, I don't want to rush, and I want to give a bit more detailed answers than just a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it as good as we can to the point, and we'll see how it happens.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, in your paragraph 7 of your statement -- do you have your statement before you? It might be useful if you have that before you.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, the ICTY statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 285A.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You should have paragraph 7 before you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you refer there to your being a director of a local utility company and having to send all your invoices to Kraljevo in Serbia. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what kind of invoices you're talking about there.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is how it was. In late November of 1991, a large group of reservists came to Kalinovik, led by a first-class captain whose name I can't remember, captain of the JNA. They were housed in the barracks in the north of Kalinovik, and we used to supply water to them through our waterworks company. So we would invoice through the federal secretariat for national defence, through the military post in Kraljevo, all of the water they used, and these funds were transferred to the account of my company. So these were the services that we provided to them. I, being in the post that I was, was able to have contacts with them in the encampment. I had contacts with the first-class captain, who was their commander there. There were --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but my question was: What were the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond invoices -- what invoices were you talking about? So again, this is an example of you really don't have to go into this level of detail. Otherwise, this could take a very long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only for you for the weekend, Mr. Hadzic; it's also because these trials take a lot of time, and the parties know exactly what details they would like to know. So, for example, if you would say these were invoices for delivery of water, then that would be fine. And Ms. Loukas will know whether it's important to know whether they were ever paid or not. So if further details -- if we need further details, she'll certainly ask you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, you've also indicated in paragraph 7 there that you say you know that these were Serbian units because you sent these invoices for water to Kraljevo. So you've -- just to clarify this: You've based your opinion that these were Serbian units on the delivery of these invoices for the water to Kraljevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also based on the contacts I had with people, with the members of that group who told me that they were from Serbia, and almost all of them were of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So they weren't all of Serbian ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They told me that most of them were. I met only one who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just going on to paragraph 9. You've indicated there that you noticed that the uniforms and insignia that they wore were not the usual JNA style. When do you say you noticed this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that, that in addition to the five-pointed star, these soldiers also had a two-headed eagle and other insignia. And they didn't wear the caps with that insignia very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. The question was when you noticed that. And of course, you should not forget, we read your whole statement, so we have a lot of information about what you already said during interviews. But Ms. Loukas specifically would like to know when you noticed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed that at that moment, when those units arrived, and later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you first notice it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those units arrived in Kalinovik in 1991. I think that it was November, or perhaps October. I know that snow was on the ground in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You've referred in your statement to the usual JNA style. What do you say is the usual JNA style?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual JNA insignia was a five-pointed star, and the officers also had their rank insignia, and later on they would have emblems indicating that on their shirts and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, these new uniforms, you say, as far back as 1991, had double-headed eagles on them; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These people who came, they had that, and also on their chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to paragraph 14 of your statement, you've referred there to the SDS and the SDA clashing. Now, is that information you've heard from other people or is that information that you were able to witness yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, these conflicts that came about started taking place in 1992, when they voted in the Assembly that Kalinovik should belong to SAO Trebinje. Then the Muslim and other members left that session and this is where the split occurred between the SDS and the SDA concerning this transfer of the territory under the jurisdiction of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could just answer my question, Mr. Hadzic. Is that information that's contained there in relation to paragraph 14 information that you witnessed yourself, information you're giving from witnessing it yourself, or information that you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, so I didn't see it, but I heard about it from the SDA leadership or the SDS leadership, that they had a disagreement. And then later on, various citizens' associations started getting involved in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going on to paragraph 16, Mr. Hadzic. You indicate there that -- you give some evidence in relation to the arming of the Serb population, and you were asked some questions about that earlier today by Mr. Gaynor. And it would be correct to state that the basis of what you say in paragraph 16 is that you saw a military truck go to a house a hundred metres from a water pipe, and that house was a house in which Serbs lived, and that there were also a lot of weapons around, being shot into the air by Serbians around the period of Serbian Christmas and new year in early 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to paragraph 21, you've indicated there that the Serb police were making arrests for no reason whatsoever, and you've given an example there that two of your friends, Tahir Panjeta and Paso Mrzic were detained at the police station for about 15 days and then released without charge. Now, are you aware of what the reason was given at the time to your friends for their detention at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the reason, nor did they know a reason for their detention at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay: Are you able to give the Trial Chamber examples of -- or names of other people who were arrested, other than the two of your friends that you've indicated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [Resumed]
